sections.heading: Seeing you as the eternal God
sections.text: Great I AM, lift my eyes above the smallness of my days. Help me sit with the wonder that time does not carry you along the way it carries me. Nations rise and fall, generations pass, whole worlds change, but you are not shaken, worn down, surprised, or diminished. You are alive forever, full of glory, and always yourself.
theological_themes: God is eternal, unchanging, and infinitely greater than creation.
Human history and earthly powers are temporary, but God remains steady and glorious.

scripture_references.connection: Moses contrasts human frailty with God’s eternal being, grounding worship in the truth that God is God before, during, and after every generation.
Peter reminds believers that God is not bound by time as we are, which supports the prayer’s awe before the One for whom human measures of time are not ultimate.
James speaks of God as the giver who has no shifting or shadow of change, directly illuminating the prayer’s confidence in God’s unchanging nature.

sections.heading: Resting in you when everything else gives way
sections.text: Father, teach me to be glad that when people die, you live; when everything I lean on cracks under my weight, you do not. So much around me promises fullness and then leaves me thirsty. Beauty fades, strength fails, plans change, and comforts run dry. But you are solid ground under my feet, and in Christ you give the water my soul actually needs.
theological_themes: Created things are fragile and unable to satisfy the soul as God does.
God alone is dependable, and Christ is the believer’s true life and satisfaction.

scripture_references.connection: God rebukes his people for forsaking him, the fountain of living waters, and turning to broken cisterns. This grounds the prayer’s contrast between God’s fullness and the emptiness of false supports.
Isaiah sets human frailty against the enduring word of God, supporting the prayer’s recognition that created life fades while God remains trustworthy.
Jesus offers living water that truly satisfies, which clarifies why the prayer turns from empty earthly sources to lasting life in Christ.

sections.heading: Turning from passing things to Christ
sections.text: Turn my heart away from empty distractions, restless dissatisfaction, and the insecurity of this present life. Anchor me in what lasts: belonging to Christ, being found in him, and having my future bound up with him. Do not let me spend myself on what cannot keep me. Make Christ my treasure, my safety, and my lasting hope.
theological_themes: Repentance includes turning from vanity and misplaced hopes to Christ.
The believer’s deepest and most lasting interest is union with Christ and eternal life in him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul counts all things as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him, which closely supports the prayer’s desire to be moved from lesser securities to Christ himself.
Paul tells believers to set their minds on things above because their life is hidden with Christ in God, grounding the prayer’s turn from the passing present to eternal life in Christ.

sections.heading: Using a short life for love and mercy
sections.text: Remind me that my life is brief and I do not know how much time I have. Let that not make me frantic, but faithful. Give me an eager, holy urgency to use the time you give me well. Wake me up when there is good to do: to feed the hungry, clothe those in need, teach those who do not know the truth, help people turn back from destructive sin, forgive those who wrong me, share the gospel, and show practical love to every neighbor you put in my path.
theological_themes: Human life is short and uncertain, so time should be used faithfully before God.
Christian usefulness includes mercy, forgiveness, instruction, evangelism, and neighbor-love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to walk wisely and make the best use of the time, which supports the prayer’s urgency to use a brief life for obedience and love.
Jesus identifies care for the hungry, the stranger, the unclothed, and the needy as service rendered to him, grounding the prayer’s concrete acts of mercy.

Paul calls spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in sin with gentleness and to bear one another’s burdens, supporting the prayer’s desire to help people turn from destructive ways without pride.
The risen Christ commissions his people to make disciples and teach his commands, which grounds the prayer’s desire to spread the gospel and instruct others in the truth.

sections.heading: Living dependent on you, not myself
sections.text: Keep me from trusting myself as though I were strong enough on my own. Teach me to depend on you in everything. Put to death what is sinful in me. Join my daily life more deeply to the cross of Christ, so that my pride, selfishness, and love of ease do not rule me. Make me a person of prayer—honest, needy, watchful, and near to you.
theological_themes: The Christian life is lived by dependence on God rather than confidence in the self.
Sanctification involves putting sin to death and living in fellowship with the crucified Christ.
Prayer is the posture of a needy believer who relies on God.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing, directly supporting the prayer’s desire for self-distrust and dependence on God.
Paul says believers put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit, which grounds the prayer’s request for real mortification of sin rather than mere self-improvement.
Paul describes the believer as crucified with Christ and now living by faith in him, illuminating the prayer’s desire for a life shaped by Christ’s cross.
Paul’s brief command to pray without ceasing supports the prayer’s closing desire to live in continual dependence and communion with God.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase “holy avarice” uses the language of greed positively to describe zeal for redeeming time. I avoided the word “greed” in the prayer text because it would likely mislead contemporary readers, but preserved the idea as eager, holy urgency.

The original phrases “instruct the ignorant” and “reclaim the vicious” are morally direct and culturally blunt. I rendered them as teaching those who do not know the truth and helping people turn from destructive sin, aiming to preserve the moral seriousness without making the prayer sound contemptuous.

The original’s language of “mortification” and “crucifixion” can be misunderstood today as self-hatred or bodily harm. I interpreted it in the Pauline sense of putting sin to death and living by union with Christ in his cross.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated “an eternal interest in Christ” as belonging to Christ, being found in him, and having one’s lasting hope secured in him, rather than as a vague interest in religious things.

I interpreted the prayer’s contrast between dying people, failing creatures, and the living Lord as a call to detach trust from created supports and place it in God himself, not as a rejection of creaturely goods as evil.

I kept the original movement from contemplation of God’s infinity, to the instability of created life, to Christ as lasting hope, to urgent usefulness, and finally to a life of dependence, repentance, and prayer.
